Weapon
WEP-un
n. (an instrument of offence in combat; rendering Hebrew keli, nesheq, Greek hoplon)
Old English waepen, of Germanic origin. Where armour is what a soldier wears, a weapon is what he uses; Scripture is emphatic that the Christian has both, and that neither is made of steel.

Biblical Definition

A weapon is an instrument of offence, and the New Testament's central statement about Christian weapons is a denial followed by a claim: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Both halves matter. Not carnal rules out coercion, political force, manipulation, and the whole apparatus of worldly leverage. Mighty through God rules out the pious weakness that mistakes having no sword for having no power. Paul then names the target with precision: the strong holds are arguments and pretensions — “casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). The battlefield is the mind, the fortress is a false idea, and the weapon that reduces it is the truth. Isaiah gives the corresponding promise on the defensive side, and it is a promise about outcome rather than about exemption: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn” (Isaiah 54:17). Weapons are formed and tongues do rise; what is denied is not the attack but its success. And Ecclesiastes adds the sober counterweight that one sinner destroys much good — the wisdom that is better than weapons of war can still be undone from within.

Webster 1828 Definition

An instrument of offence. Paul denies that Christian weapons are carnal and claims they are mighty through God, aimed at arguments and pretensions; Isaiah promises not that no weapon will be formed but that none will prosper.

expand to see more

WEAPON, n. wep'n. [Sax. waepen.] Any instrument of offense; any thing used or designed to be used in destroying or annoying an enemy.

2. An instrument for contest, or for annoying an enemy. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. 2 Cor. 10.

3. In botany, a thorn, prickle or sting, with which plants are furnished.

4. Weapon-salve, a salve which was supposed to cure the wound by being applied to the weapon that made it.

5. Figuratively, any means of attack or defense, as words or arguments.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 10:4 — "(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)"

2 Corinthians 10:5 — "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;"

Isaiah 54:17 — "No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD."

Ecclesiastes 7:12 — "For wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 54:17 is preached as a personal shield against all adversity, detaching it from the servants of the LORD it was given to and from the judgment-scene it describes; and 2 Corinthians 10:4 is quoted to bless whichever weapons the speaker already prefers.

expand to see more

“No weapon formed against me shall prosper” has become a talisman, recited over careers, finances, and health as a guarantee that nothing will go wrong. The verse says something better and narrower. Its setting is a courtroom — every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment — and its subject is stated at the end: the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me. The promise is that no accusation will finally stand against those whose righteousness God has supplied, which is the same ground Paul stands on when he asks who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect (Romans 8:33). It does not promise that no weapon will be formed; Isaiah has just said in the previous clause that God creates the waster to destroy. It promises the verdict, not the absence of the trial — and every martyr in Hebrews 11 died with the promise intact.

2 Corinthians 10:4 suffers the reverse abuse: it is cited to endorse whatever the speaker was going to do anyway. For one camp it sanctifies retreat, as though non-carnal meant non-confrontational, when Paul in the same breath speaks of pulling down and casting down. For another it becomes a warrant for spiritual-warfare technique — binding, rebuking, and territorial mapping — that Paul never describes. His own account of the weapon is unglamorous and specific: arguments demolished, thoughts brought captive to Christ's obedience. That is preaching, teaching, apologetic, and discipline, exercised by ordinary men with an open Bible, and it is more powerful than any of the substitutes offered for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew keli (implement, hence weapon) and nesheq (armament); Greek hoplon (an implement or weapon), whose plural gives both armour in Romans 13:12 and weapons in 2 Corinthians 10:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew keli (H3627) — article, implement, weapon; the general word for equipment of any kind.

Hebrew nesheq (H5402) — weaponry, armament; the collective term for a nation's arms.

Greek hoplon (G3696) — a tool, implement, weapon; plural hopla, rendered weapons in 2 Corinthians 10:4 and instruments in Romans 6:13.

Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; the adjective Paul denies of Christian weapons.

Greek ochyroma (G3794) — a stronghold, fortress; the target in 2 Corinthians 10:4, which verse 5 identifies as arguments and pretensions.

Usage

"“The weapons of our warfare are not carnal” — a denial and a claim: no worldly leverage, and no powerlessness either."

"“Bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” — the mind is the battlefield and the objective."

"“No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” — the verdict is promised, not the absence of the trial."
